persons.name: Tom
persons.harm: A friend of four years, released on bond, used invented bail, hospital and homelessness crises (and a fake 'mom') between May and July 2023 to get Venmo and Zelle payments, his card and bank details, and a credit card opened in his name. A community member estimated his losses at about $15,000. The show notes he founded a disability advocacy group, and it raises whether he was targeted because of disability.
persons.perpetrator_role: a friend; the season's con artist

quotes.quote: It's a civil matter, not a criminal matter anyway.
I can't afford lawyers for crud and I'm not going to go to my parents for that because they've supported me through a lot.
I really wouldn't want to know that their son was foolish enough to get himself in a situation like this.

contacts.what_was_asked: To deal with unexplained charges on his card
contacts.what_institution_did: Reversed 10 to 20 fraudulent charges in June and issued several replacement cards. He later changed his bank account.
contacts.quote: I would say there were between 10 or 20 charges that my bank reversed in that month alone, and I was able to get that money back.
contacts.what_happened_next: Believing it was ordinary identity theft, he kept giving new card and account details to the perpetrator. The Venmo and Zelle transfers and the credit card in his name were not recovered.
contacts.notes: The bank treated the charges as card fraud. Tom did not yet know the perpetrator was behind them.

contacts.what_was_asked: Further charges based on the evidence and testimony the podcast had gathered
contacts.what_institution_did: Met the host. At the season's end, law enforcement was described as still considering further charges. No charge for Tom's losses is reported.
contacts.quote: Last week I met with the Indiana State Police to present the evidence and testimony we've collected thus far this season. It all went really well. That's really all I can share for now.
contacts.what_happened_next: Host, finale: 'I had productive conversations with Indiana law enforcement who are still considering further charges' (s22-e12 @ 23:45).
contacts.notes: The show never says outright that Tom's case was among the evidence presented. I linked it because the host says Tom 'supplied a significant amount of organized evidence' (s22-e11 @ 22:38), and the host says other victims 'have connected with the state police'. Low certainty.

persons.outcome_quote: He's in some really financial crisis right now.
persons.decisive_work_quote: I would say there were between 10 or 20 charges that my bank reversed in that month alone, and I was able to get that money back.
persons.time_to_first_effective_action: within June 2023, the same month he reported the charges
persons.notes: The only protection was the bank reversing some card charges. The perpetrator was never charged over Tom. She was arrested in September 2023 on the rental-scam warrant, 'not even for crimes that she had committed against him' (s22-e8 @ 29:56). His contacts with the perpetrator ended when he found the scam-awareness page on July 9, 2023. Texts were read on air, and he shared bank statements with a community member. In a recorded jail call the perpetrator admitted opening a credit card in his name (s22-e9 @ 16:37). An anonymous Twitter Space speaker who lost money, lost a job and mentions disability (s22-e8 @ 39:24) may be Tom, but the show does not say so.

persons.harm: In 2021, at about 70, she paid $1,800 to sublet the perpetrator's apartment, never got keys or a refund, became homeless, and had to move to Arizona to live with a friend.

The court-ordered restitution amounts (1,300 and 600) do not match her $1,800 loss. I therefore coded her separately from the three charged complainants (P03) and coded reach as unclear.

persons.harm: A Minneapolis photographer who in 2020 invested almost all her savings (tens of thousands of dollars) with a fiduciary financial advisor. He faked her account portal and stole the money as part of a $2.3 million fraud on at least 23 clients.
persons.perpetrator_role: her financial advisor

contacts.institution: State investigator (agency not named) working the case after the advisor turned himself in to the FBI
contacts.what_was_asked: Information and getting her money back
contacts.what_institution_did: Connected her with an investigator, who interviewed her and collected her texts, emails and portal screenshots. No one would confirm to her that she had been defrauded.
contacts.quote: I ended up talking to somebody. I basically started telling my story on the phone and she was like, oh, I know exactly who this is. I guess she had gotten some other calls or something, or she was just familiar with this case. And so she ended up getting me connected with one of the investigators who had
contacts.what_happened_next: Charges, a guilty plea and sentencing followed.
contacts.notes: She found the office herself. The advisor had texted her: 'I've turned myself into the FBI.'

contacts.what_institution_did: Mailed a coping pamphlet. Otherwise she had to chase information herself.
contacts.quote: They sent me a pamphlet in the mail of things to do to like cope with being defrauded. The things on there were sort of like ridiculous. They were just so unhelpful.
contacts.what_happened_next: 'The victim advocate I had really wasn't helping me through that process' (@ 21:59).

contacts.institution: Court / prosecution (federal or state not specified)
contacts.what_institution_did: Charged him and accepted his guilty plea. Sentenced him to about seven years with restitution, and liquidated some assets for victims.
contacts.quote: He ended up being sentenced to about seven years of prison time.
contacts.what_happened_next: He was given months before reporting to prison. The asset distribution took over a year and returned 'a really small amount of money'.

persons.outcome_quote: That took a really long time though, like over a year, and distributed it amongst the victims, but it was a really small amount of money.
persons.decisive_work_quote: sometime that winter they end up charging him and they do look kind of like a virtual hearing, which I was able to go to and then he did end up pleading guilty.
persons.time_to_first_effective_action: charged 'sometime that winter', within months of her first contact in late 2020; sentenced summer 2021
persons.notes: evidence_types: the conviction backs her account; the institutional responses themselves rest on her account. A conviction was delivered, but the money she sought was mostly not recovered, hence partly_protected. The case was set off by the advisor turning himself in; how the investigation began before that is not described. The advisor's name was spoken on air and is not recorded here.

persons.name: John Cornelius McGee
persons.harm: Shot and killed in his Ohio home in 2002 by someone who kicked in the front door. The case remains unsolved. His daughter Madison, told as a child that he died of a heart attack, learned of the murder at 16 and has investigated it as a podcaster.
persons.perpetrator_role: unknown killer (police have a main suspect)

contacts.institution: Ohio police department that handled the case
contacts.what_institution_did: Identified a suspect through weak witness testimony. Produced a thin investigation, without interviews of many people or the evidence collection his daughter expected.
contacts.quote: They were able to identify a suspect through witness testimony that was not as reliable as one would hope.
contacts.what_happened_next: The suspect was taken to a grand jury.
contacts.notes: Daughter: 'This lack of evidence, this lack of investigation, not interviewing people at the time' (@ 33:36).

contacts.what_institution_did: Took the suspect to a grand jury, found the evidence insufficient, and dropped the charges.
contacts.quote: They took a person to the grand jury to see if there was enough to take it all the way to trial. They decided that they didn't have enough and they dropped the charges on this suspect.
contacts.what_happened_next: 'It's just sat for 22 years.'

contacts.institution: County records office and prosecutor's office (case-file request)
contacts.what_was_asked: A copy of the police case file
contacts.what_institution_did: Promised the file in about two and a half weeks. It arrived about eight months later, after she went over the clerk's head.
contacts.quote: My initial contact was May of 2020 and I received the files in January of 2021.
contacts.what_happened_next: She received a 36-page file with 'so many avenues that don't feel like they were explored'.
contacts.notes: She was told FOIA did not apply.

contacts.what_institution_did: Still calls the original man its number-one suspect, but has taken no new step.
contacts.quote: To this day, the police still tell me that that's their number one suspect. But that seems so strange to just let this person run around in your town and in your county if you think they murdered someone.
contacts.what_happened_next: Her podcast now draws public tips; the case is unsolved.

persons.outcome_quote: Since then, there's been no new evidence brought up. There's been no new information that they've uncovered. It's just sat for 22 years.
persons.notes: From a 'WCN Presents' interview episode included in the season's file. His name comes from the closing dedication. His daughter obtained and read the police file herself. Family acting for him (his daughter) counts as acting for the person.

coder_notes: Season 22 covers a young Indiana con artist and serial liar ('the perpetrator') through 13 numbered episodes plus a trailer and a 'WCN Presents' interview (Madison McGhee) that sits in the season files. Most harms are financial fraud, impersonation and false accusations rather than intimate abuse. Many contributors are community members and political acquaintances who say they are not victims. I described them by role and gave them no records. One of them, Alyssa, had items taken from her porch and was threatened with a CPS call, but says 'I'm not a victim' (s22-e10 @ 42:11), so I made no record for her. The only conviction (two felony counts) covers three rental-scam complainants (P03); every other harm went uncharged, ended in unpaid civil judgments, or never reached an institution. Capture after she absconded depended on stings by a citizen Facebook group, and the host presented evidence to Indiana State Police in November 2024 with further charges still 'being considered' at the end. Naming: the instructions say both to use the show's name for each harmed person and never to name an accused person. I resolved this by describing everyone the perpetrator falsely accused of crimes by role (two pastors, a statehouse staffer, a massage practitioner, a chiropractor). The House Speaker is named only inside a verbatim quotation in others_mentioned. Inside every quotation the perpetrator's name is replaced with [perpetrator]; nothing else in the quotations is changed. The Celisia Stanton advisor's name, spoken on air, is not recorded. Context: when this run resumed after a usage-limit interruption, the output folder held only TASK.md, so notes.md was rebuilt from scratch while reading. All eight chunk files were read to their last lines.
